subjects.name: Police unions in the United States

summary: Part five of the Behind the Police series traces how US police professionalised and then unionised, winning contracts that purge misconduct records and reinstate fired officers, and how broken windows and stop-and-frisk policing targeted Black and Latino Americans.

evidence.note: narrative starts at the turn of the 20th century with police as muscle for political machines
August Vollmer becomes Berkeley police chief in 1909 and drives professionalisation
1919 Boston police strike after officers seek an AFL charter; Coolidge bans public safety strikes
New York PBA becomes a bargaining union in the 1960s and fights the 1966 civilian review board
contract clauses purging disciplinary records and research linking bargaining rights to killings
segment on Minneapolis union head Bob Kroll, his complaints and alleged white power patch
unions block reform by elected officials in St. Louis and Minneapolis
1982 Atlantic article launches broken windows theory and its misuse of Zimbardo's study
Wilson's biological theories of crime and ties to the authors of The Bell Curve
NYPD slowdown after Eric Garner's death and the study showing major crime complaints fell

notes: Fifth of a six-part Behind the Police miniseries, packaged as its own story. Primary subject is US police unions as a whole, entered as an organization with org_type police; no single named union fits. Early-1900s corruption and Vollmer professionalisation open the covered span (approximate start 1900). Bob Kroll has no reliable birth year, so floruit is used. Transcript year digits are often garbled.
